query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A physics‐informed, machine learning–based predictive model that explicitly incorporates realistic defect features – notably oxygen impurities – can more accurately predict the temperature‐dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr in both the low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) regimes than current analytical models based on ideal, defect-free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr, as synthesized with typical processing‐induced defects and containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a machine learning framework that uses training data from experiments (including conductivity measurements on specimens with 1 wt.% oxygen) and simulated structural data featuring realistic defect distributions, then use this model to predict the conductivity over the target temperature regimes.
generation.conditions: Measurements and predictions are considered over two distinct regimes: a low-temperature region (0–200 K) where quantum and defect‐induced localization effects may dominate, and a high-temperature region (300–1200 K) where phonon and impurity scattering control conductivity. The sample state is that of a non-ideal, defect-containing bulk alloy with ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence and distribution of oxygen-induced defects (and their interaction with the inherent high-entropy microstructure) which modify the electronic density of states and influence electron scattering rates.
generation.mechanism: By accounting for the contributions of point defects, oxygen clusters, and associated localized states through data-driven adjustments of electron scattering parameters, the ML model can capture non-ideal effects omitted in perfect-crystal analytical theories. This leads to more realistic predictions of carrier mobility, particularly capturing enhanced scattering at low temperatures and the combined phonon–impurity scattering at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Predicted electrical conductivity curves that closely match experimental measurements (with deviations within ~10–20% rather than ~30% or more as typical of idealized analytical models) across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes, and that reflect distinct scattering mechanisms between the regimes.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions based on perfect, defect-free crystal approximations that do not account for oxygen impurities or other microstructural defects.
generation.boundary: The model is expected to be accurate for bulk samples of HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels on the order of 1 wt.% and within the temperature windows of approximately 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Deviations in oxygen content or samples with significant microstructural changes due to extreme processing may lie outside the model’s applicability.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in quantitatively modeling the precise distribution and electronic effects of oxygen-induced defects, especially in the 0–200 K regime where quantum effects can further complicate scattering. The relative contributions of defect versus phonon scattering might also vary outside the trained conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens with controlled oxygen content (~1 wt.%) and measure their electrical conductivity at benchmark temperatures (e.g., 0 K (as extrapolated), 150 K, 300 K, 600 K, and 900 K) using standard 4-point probe methods under well-controlled conditions. Compare the results with the predictions from the ML model. Experiments should also examine changes in microstructural features (via TEM/EDS) to confirm the defect distribution assumed by the model.
measurements: Electrical conductivity at multiple temperatures (e.g., 150, 300, 600, 900 K)
Microstructural characterization of defect and oxygen distributions (TEM, EDS, XRD)
Comparison of activation energies inferred from the temperature dependence of conductivity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based predictions of electrical conductivity deviate by more than 20% from the experimental measurements at any of the benchmark temperatures, or if the predicted changes in conduction mechanisms between the low and high temperature regimes (e.g., a clear transition in activation energy) are not observed, then the hypothesis that the defect-informed ML model improves prediction accuracy over analytical approaches is falsified.

The Effect of Electronic Structure on the Phases Present in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractMulticomponent systems, termed High Entropy Alloys (HEAs), with predominantly single solid solution phases are a current area of focus in alloy development. Although different empirical rules have been introduced to understand phase formation and determine what the dominant phases may be in these systems, experimental investigation has revealed that in many cases their structure is not a single solid solution phase, and that the rules may not accurately distinguish the stability of the phase boundaries. Here, a combined modelling and experimental approach that looks into the electronic structure is proposed to improve accuracy of the predictions of the majority phase. To do this, the Rigid Band model is generalised for magnetic systems in prediction of the majority phase most likely to be found. Good agreement is found when the predictions are confronted with data from experiments, including a new magnetic HEA system (CoFeNiV). A comparison of explainable artificial intelligence methods in the phase classification of multi-principal element alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe demonstrate the capabilities of two model-agnostic local post-hoc model interpretability methods, namely breakDown (BD) and shapley (SHAP), to explain the predictions of a black-box classification learning model that establishes a quantitative relationship between chemical composition and multi-principal element alloys (MPEA) phase formation. We trained an ensemble of support vector machines using a dataset with 1,821 instances, 12 features with low pair-wise correlation, and seven phase labels. Feature contributions to the model prediction are computed by BD and SHAP for each composition. The resulting BD and SHAP transformed data are then used as inputs to identify similar composition groups using k-means clustering. Explanation-of-clusters by features reveal that the results from SHAP agree more closely with the literature. Visualization of compositions within a cluster using Ceteris-Paribus (CP) profile plots show the functional dependencies between the feature values and predicted response.
